title: The Weaver of Endings
summary: High in a tower, an old woman weaves the ending of every story in the world on an endless loom. When Lino climbs up to beg a happy ending for his sick mother's story, he discovers that the weaver does not choose the endings — and that the power to change them may lie in a hand much closer than he imagined.

chapters.title: The Tower at the Edge of the Map
chapters.body:
They said, in Lino's village, that at the edge of the world there was a tower, and that inside it an old woman wove the ending of every story.

It was a story told to children, and Lino had stopped believing it around the age of ten, along with the other bedtime tales. But Lino was now thirteen, and his mother was ill — very ill, with the illness the doctors speak of in low voices and from which the grown-ups avert their eyes — and when your life begins to turn into a sad story, you go back to believing anything that promises a different ending.

So Lino went to find the tower.

It took weeks. He crossed the forest that lay beyond the village, and the fields that lay beyond the forest, and the desert of stone that lay beyond the fields, always heading west, to where the map had no more names, only the blank of places no one has visited. And when he had all but decided the tower was only a children's tale, it appeared: tall, slender, made of bone-colored stone, rising from the empty ground until it was lost in the clouds. No door at the bottom. Only a spiral staircase on the outside, climbing, climbing.

Lino climbed. It took the whole day. And at the top, in a round room open to the sky on every side, he found the weaver.

She was older than anyone Lino had ever seen — old as the stones, old as time itself. And before her was a loom so vast it was lost to sight, with millions upon millions of threads of every color, coming and going, and she wove without stopping, with fingers that moved far too quickly for her age.

"You've come far, boy," she said, without stopping her weaving, without turning. "Few make it. Would you like water? The climb is hard."

"Are you the weaver?" Lino asked, out of breath. "The one who weaves the ending of stories?"

"I am," she said. "Every thread on this loom is a life. Every life is a story. And I weave the ending of each one." She nodded toward the endless loom. "That golden thread there belongs to a girl who will become a queen. That grey thread is a man who will die tomorrow without knowing it. That red thread, crossing with the blue one, is two who will love each other all their lives. I weave it all. Every ending. It has been my craft since before there were names for things."

Lino's heart raced. It was true. The children's tale was true. And if the old woman wove the endings, then she could change one.

"Please," he said, and fell to his knees, because he had come so far and carried so much. "My mother is ill. Her story is going to end badly. I know it. The doctors know it. Everyone knows it and no one says it." The tears came. "You weave the endings. So please, I beg you: weave a happy ending for her. Make her well. You can. You have the power. Just one thread. Just one different ending. It's all I ask."

chapters.title: The Weaver Who Does Not Choose
chapters.body:
The old woman stopped weaving. It was the first time, and the silence of the stopped loom filled the tower like a heavy thing.

She turned, at last, and looked at Lino with eyes that had seen the beginning and the end of everything, and in them was a sadness so vast and so gentle that Lino felt, before she spoke, that the answer would not be the one he wanted.

"Boy," she said, very tenderly. "I must tell you a truth that will be hard to hear." She laid her old hands in her lap. "I weave the endings. But I do not choose them."

"What do you mean?" Lino didn't understand. "You're the one who makes them. You just said so."

"I weave what the threads bring me," she said. "Every thread comes to me already with its color, already with its path. I only cross them, fasten them, finish them — I give shape to the ending that a person's life has been building, choice by choice, day by day. I am the weaver, not the author. Each person's story is written by that person, and by everyone who crosses their life, over all their days. By the time the thread reaches my loom, it is already what it is. I cannot change the color of a thread, boy. I can only weave it honestly." She shook her head, slowly. "If I lied — if I wove an ending that life had not built — the whole cloth of the world would unravel. An ending must be true, or it is not an ending, only a lie that collapses."

Lino felt the ground vanish. He had come so far. He had crossed forests and deserts. And the weaver, his one hope, was saying she could do nothing.

"Then there's no way," he whispered, and his voice broke. "My mother's story will end badly and no one can change it."

"I did not say that," said the old woman, and there was something in her eyes now, a glimmer, almost. "I said that I cannot change it. That the ending is written by life, not by me." She leaned toward Lino. "But your mother's life hasn't ended yet, has it? Her thread hasn't reached my loom. It is still being woven, down there, in the world, by her and by all who love her. And while a thread is still being made, boy, its color can still change. Not by my hand. By the hands of those who live the story."

She rose, with effort, and led Lino to the edge of the open room, from which the whole world could be seen far below, small and distant.

"Let me show you something almost no one understands," she said. "People climb this tower asking me to change their ending, as if the ending were something that falls from the sky, finished, with no part of their own in it. But the ending of a story is not the last chapter, boy. The ending is the sum of everything that came before. It is made of each day, each choice, each act of love or of giving up." She pointed down, at the world. "You don't change the ending of your mother's story by climbing up here and begging me. You change her ending down there, at her side, living each day that remains as full of love as you can. That is what weaves a good ending. Not my hand up here. Your hands down there."

chapters.title: The Thread in the Hand of the Living
chapters.body:
Lino looked at the world far below, and then at the old woman, and something began to settle inside him — slowly, painfully, but truly.

"But what if…" he hesitated, because the question hurt. "What if, even so, she dies? If I go back, and stay at her side, and love her every day, and her story still ends badly? Then I'll have done it all for nothing."

The old woman looked at him with infinite tenderness, and was slow to answer, because the answer was the most important of all.

"Boy," she said. "Let me ask you something. A story in which a mother falls ill, and her son, instead of fleeing the suffering, stays at her side to the end, loving her in every day that remains, making her laugh, holding her hand, saying all that needs to be said — that story, even if the mother dies, is it a sad story?" She shook her head slowly. "It is sad, yes. But it is also one of the most beautiful stories there are. An ending can be sad and beautiful at the same time. It can break the heart and still be a good ending — the best possible ending for that story."

She took Lino's hands in hers, old and warm.

"What makes a story end badly is not the sadness. It is not the loss. Those things come to everyone, sooner or later; I weave more sad endings than you imagine, and many of them are lovely. What makes a story truly end badly is regret. It is reaching the end and thinking, 'I could have loved more, and I didn't.' 'I could have stayed, and I fled.' 'I had the time, and I wasted it on fear.'" She squeezed his hands. "You came all this way, to the edge of the world, to try to save your mother. That tells me you love her very much. So go back, boy. Run back. Don't waste the time that remains climbing towers and begging old women. Every day you spend far from her searching for a miracle is a day you could be weaving, with your own hands, the most beautiful ending possible — an ending without regret, full to the brim with love."

Lino wept. But it was a different weeping from when he had climbed up — not of despair, but of understanding.

"I wanted so much for her to get well," he whispered.

"I know," said the old woman. "And perhaps she will; I don't know, her thread hasn't come to me yet, and not everything that seems lost is. But whatever the color of the thread, you still hold in your hands the power to make her ending a good one. Not by curing her — that may not be within your reach. But by loving her in a way that, when the end comes, whatever it is, leaves neither of you with any 'I wish I had.' That is the one miracle that was always in your hands, and never in mine."

Lino dried his eyes. He stood. And he bowed to the old weaver, from the bottom of his heart.

"Thank you," he said. "I climbed up thinking you would change the ending. And you did something better. You reminded me that the ending is still mine to weave."

"Go," said the old woman, and she smiled, and her smile was that of someone who has woven this ending a thousand times and is still moved by it. "Run. And boy—" she called, as he was already going down, "when you get home, don't waste time grieving what hasn't happened yet. Spend each day as if it were a golden thread. Because it is."

Lino ran down the tower, and crossed the desert, and the fields, and the forest, faster than he had come, because now each day had a value he hadn't known before. And he reached home, and went into the room where his mother lay resting, pale and tired but alive, and she opened her eyes and smiled at the sight of him, and asked where on earth he had been all this time.

And Lino did not tell her about the tower, nor the weaver. He only climbed onto the bed beside her, and held her hand, and said:

"I went very far to find a way to help you, Mom. And I found out the way was this. To stay. At your side." He rested his head on her shoulder. "Tell me a story. One of the old ones. And I'm not going anywhere."

What happened to Lino's mother, this story does not tell — because her ending was not being woven in a tower at the edge of the world, but, day after day, in a small room where a boy learned to love without wasting an hour. Whether she got well or not is the least important thing. What matters is that, whatever the color of that thread when it finally reached the old woman's loom, it arrived without a single knot of regret — woven whole, from both sides, with the love of a mother and a son who knew, in time, that the ending of a story is made by the hands of those who live it.

And that, the weaver would say, is the happiest any ending can be.
